title: Alexandropol to Fontainebleau: The Way of the Seeker of Truth
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Hearth at the Edge of Empires

stops.name: Alexandropol (Gyumri), the Greek quarter
stops.campa: In the Greek quarter of Alexandropol, on the frozen rim where three empires grind together, a son is born to Ioannis Giorgiades, a Greek carpenter, cattle-owner, and ashokh, and his Armenian wife Evdokia. The night itself is disputed: the family keeps New Year's Eve, the passport will one day say another year entirely, and the fog around the date is the first of his mysteries. The house smells of wood shavings and wool; Turkish, Armenian, Greek and Russian are spoken across a single supper table.

stops.name: Alexandropol, the grandmother's deathbed
stops.campa: His grandmother, past a hundred years old, calls the boy to her deathbed, lays her hand on his head, and binds him with her last strength: in life, never do as others do, either do nothing, only go to school, or do what nobody else does. The command enters him like a seed. At the forty-day grave rite he scandalizes the mourners by hopping around the grave and singing a rhyme of his own making; the injunction is already at work.
stops.quote: In life never do as others do... Either do nothing — just go to school — or do something nobody else does.
stops.quote_source: The grandmother's injunction as Gurdjieff records it, Beelzebub's Tales to His Grandson, 'The Arousing of Thought'
sources: Beelzebub's Tales to His Grandson, 'The Arousing of Thought'

stops.name: Alexandropol, the Yezidi boy in the circle
stops.campa: In a side street the boy comes upon children tormenting a small Yezidi: they have drawn a circle around him in the dust and he cannot get out. He strains against nothing at all, weeping, as against a wall. Gurdjieff rubs away part of the line and the child shoots out like a bolt. The grown men he questions shrug or lie. He tests it later and finds it true: dragged bodily from the circle, a Yezidi falls into catalepsy. No priest, no schoolmaster, no book of physics will ever explain it to him, and the wound of not-knowing stays open for life.
stops.quote: If a Yezidi is forcibly dragged out of a circle, he immediately falls into the state called catalepsy.
suggested_refs: Yezidi communities of the Armenian plateau

stops.name: Kars: the family follows the fallen fortress
stops.campa: The guns of the Tsar have taken Kars, and ruin has taken the Giorgiades herds: a cattle plague eats the family fortune in a season. The father, proud and unbowed, moves the household to the newly Russian fortress town and opens a carpenter's shop. Kars is a garrison Babel: Cossacks, Greeks, Armenians, Tatars, Molokan sectarians, all pressed inside grey basalt walls under a citadel. Here the boy will be forged, between the workshop's poverty and the cathedral's chant.
sources: James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth

stops.name: Kars, the military cathedral: Dean Borsh
stops.campa: His voice earns him a place in the choir of the fortress cathedral, and the choir brings him under the eye of Dean Borsh, master of the garrison's souls. The old priest, hearing the boy argue, takes him from the municipal school and teaches him alone: mathematics, astronomy, Latin, the making of a man. Borsh and the father sit evenings trading questions about God and the world while the boy listens from the shadows. The Dean's design is set: the boy shall be both physician of the body and confessor of the soul, for neither alone can heal a man.
stops.quote: The man who was soon to become my first tutor, the founder and creator of my present individuality, and, so to say, the 'third aspect of my inner God'.
stops.quote_source: Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'My Father' (of Dean Borsh)
suggested_refs: The Kars military cathedral (Church of the Holy Apostles)
sources: Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'My First Tutor'

stops.name: Kars, Gilgamesh by the hearth
stops.campa: Winter nights, the father sings. He is an ashokh, a contest bard who has stood against the best singers of Van and Karabagh, and among his songs is the oldest of all: the tale of Gilgamesh, carried mouth to mouth for thousands of years. The boy hears of the Flood before the Flood and does not forget a line. Decades later he will read in a magazine that tablets dug from the ruins of Nineveh carry the very verses his father sang by the hearth, proof that a song can outlast empires, passed unwritten across five thousand years, and he will weep at the confirmation.
stops.quote: I will tell thee, Gilgamesh, / Of a mournful mystery of the Gods: / How once, having met together, / They resolved to flood the land of Shuruppak.
stops.quote_source: The father's recitation as recorded in Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'My Father'
suggested_refs: The flood tablet (Tablet XI) of the Epic of Gilgamesh, British Museum
The ashokh tradition of the Transcaucasus

stops.name: The saint's tomb beyond Alexandropol: the paralytic walks and the rain falls
stops.campa: Wonders multiply and refuse the schoolbooks. A paralytic who cannot lift a spoon has himself dragged on a cart to the tomb of a saint on the hill; he kisses the stone, and before the day is out he walks back down on his own legs. In a rainless summer the whole town, Orthodox, Armenian, Muslim alike, follows the archimandrite and the icon into the parched fields; before the procession regains the gates the sky breaks open and drenches them. The boy stands in the miracle rain, counting what his physics cannot count.
suggested_refs: Pilgrimage tombs of the Shirak plateau
sources: Meetings with Remarkable Men (the chain of inexplicable events of his youth)

stops.name: Alexandropol, the table that raps
stops.campa: At his aunt's house a three-legged table answers questions, knocking out letters and numbers for the dead. A fortune-teller traces his palm and reads a wound that has not yet happened: a gun, a right side, a far country; years later the stray bullets will keep her appointment. He devours books of neurology and hypnotism, interrogates priests and doctors, and finds every explanation thinner than the facts. The choice hardens in him: he will not rest until he knows the meaning and purpose of life on earth, whatever it costs and wherever the answer hides.
suggested_refs: Séance culture of the Russian provinces, 1880s

stops.name: Tiflis, the stoker who reads Greek
stops.campa: Too restless for the seminary road laid out for him, he goes to Tiflis and shovels coal for the Transcaucasian Railway, sleeping among firemen and reading by lamp. In the city of sulphur baths and caravanserais he finds his first brothers of the search: Sarkis Pogossian, a theological student who cannot sit still, and soon Abram Yelov, the bookstall Assyrian who can find any volume in any tongue. They pool their books and their questions. The Seekers of Truth begin here, in soot and argument, before they have a name.
sources: Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'Pogossian' and 'Abram Yelov'

stops.name: Echmiadzin, the holy see that does not answer
stops.campa: With Pogossian he walks as a pilgrim to Echmiadzin, the Vatican of Armenia, where the chrism of a whole people is boiled in a cauldron once every seven years. They lodge weeks in the hostel for pilgrims, question monks, stand through the long chants under Ararat's white witness. The liturgy is magnificent and the answer is not there. He leaves with the certainty that what he seeks was known once and has been withdrawn from the open churches, driven underground, into ruins and brotherhoods. The search turns from the altar toward the buried.

stops.name: Ani, the parchments in the ruined city
stops.campa: In the dead capital of a thousand and one churches, he and Pogossian camp among the ruins and dig. Under a collapsed passage of a monastery they break into a monk's cell and find letters on parchment, monk to monk, in old Armenian. One line stops their breath: word of the Sarmoung Brotherhood, a famous esoteric school, and of where its heirs had gone. A word he has already met in the old book Merkhavat now stands in his hands with an address attached: somewhere between Urmia and Kurdistan. The digging stops; the journey begins.
stops.quote: This word is the name of a famous esoteric school which, according to tradition, was founded in Babylon.

stops.name: The road through Turkish Armenia, the map of pre-sand Egypt
stops.campa: Traveling disguised toward Mesopotamia on the trail of the Sarmoung, they shelter in the house of an Armenian priest. Among the old man's relics is a parchment map that will not let Gurdjieff sleep: Egypt drawn before the sands: the Sphinx and the great works standing in a country that has not yet been buried. He trembles as over treasure; the priest will not sell, so through a night he copies it secretly, line by line, and afterward carries the copy against his chest through bazaars and frontiers, oilcloth-wrapped, like a second heart.
suggested_refs: The map of pre-sand Egypt (Meetings with Remarkable Men)
sources: Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'Prince Yuri Lubovedsky'

stops.name: Smyrna, the brawl in the port
stops.campa: Working his way toward Egypt, he lands in Smyrna and is baptized into the fraternity of ports: a night quarrel among sailors becomes a general battle, and he wakes bruised beside new friends from a foreign fleet. The fists buy him what money could not: passage. He ships as a hand toward Alexandria, one more dark-eyed young man among the rigging, with the copied map of drowned-in-sand Egypt strapped under his shirt and a purpose no one on board could guess.

stops.name: Giza, the Sphinx, and the meeting at its paws
stops.campa: He works as a guide among the pyramids, spending his nights comparing the stones against the parchment of pre-sand Egypt. Sitting at the foot of the Sphinx, absorbed in the map, he is found by a Russian archaeologist, Professor Skridlov, and then by the man whose life will braid with his for thirty-five years: Prince Yuri Lubovedsky, who sees the map and turns pale, for he has been hunting the same trail. Guide and prince recognize each other as seekers. Egypt gives him no final answer, but it gives him his brotherhood; together they will go up the Nile to Thebes and sit among the tombs.
suggested_refs: Thebes and the Valley of the Kings
sources: Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'Prince Yuri Lubovedsky'

stops.name: Jerusalem: guide at the Holy Sepulchre
stops.campa: He earns his bread as a guide to Russian pilgrims in Jerusalem, leading peasants who have walked half a continent to kiss the Stone of Unction. He learns the city as a professional of holiness: the Easter fire, the rival monks policing inches of the Sepulchre, the trade in relics; and he studies faith itself as a force: what it does in a body, what it heals, what it blinds. The Essenes enter his research here; he will say later that among their heirs certain psalms were made to grow plants faster. The seeker files Jerusalem among the places where truth once stood and left a forwarding address.

stops.name: Crete, the first stray bullet
stops.campa: Insurrection burns across Crete, and he is on the island, the canon says on a political errand among the Greeks, when the first of his three stray bullets finds him, in the year before the Greco-Turkish war. He falls without seeing who fired. Unknown Greeks carry his unconscious body off the island, and he wakes far away, in Jerusalem, mended by strangers. It is the first of the three woundings, each of which will drop him at the door of death and each time send him back changed, as if the bullets themselves were part of the curriculum.
sources: Life Is Real Only Then, When 'I Am' (the three wounds)

stops.name: Mecca and Medina, the hajj in disguise
stops.campa: Dressed and bearded as a pilgrim, speaking the tongues he has collected like keys, he enters the forbidden cities where an unmasked unbeliever dies. He circles the Kaaba in the white flood of the hajj, stands at Medina, watches everything with the double sight of the seeker. And he concludes what he concluded at Echmiadzin and Jerusalem: the secret is not here either; the outer rite guards an emptied room. Whatever Islam keeps of the old knowledge, he decides, is kept elsewhere: in Bokhara, among the dervish orders of the east. The needle of the search swings toward Turkestan.
sources: Meetings with Remarkable Men (the Mecca-Medina reconnaissance)

stops.name: Bokhara, the reservoir of the dervishes
stops.campa: Bokhara the Noble: a hundred madrasahs, the last emirate where the muezzin's law still runs, and beneath the official piety a web of dervish lineages older than the mosques. He comes with Soloviev, the ex-drunkard he cured and converted into a brother of the search, and they burrow into the city's underlife: Sufi zikr, the science of breath, the mathematics of music. Here the trail of the Sarmoung, first read on parchment at Ani, grows warm at last: contact is made, a promise given. They wait for the guides the brotherhood will send.
sources: Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'Soloviev' and 'Prince Yuri Lubovedsky'

stops.name: The Amu Darya crossing
stops.campa: At dawn they are put onto the great river the ancients called Oxus, the water that has carried armies, prophets and smuggled knowledge for three thousand years. The ferry crawls; the yellow current tugs at the poles; on the far bank Asia deepens and the writ of every empire thins. The canon keeps this river as a threshold: beyond the Amu Darya begin the roads that do not appear on Russian maps, and the two travelers cross it the way other men cross into a church.
suggested_refs: The Oxus/Amu Darya in the geography of the search
sources: Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'Prince Yuri Lubovedsky'

stops.name: The Sarmoung Monastery, the blindfolded journey; the dances read as books
stops.campa: Four Kara-Kirghiz guides come; the condition is a vow: hoods over the eyes. Twelve days on horseback through passes, the blindfolds lifted only at rope bridges swaying over gorges. Then a valley no map names, courtyards, silence: the Sarmoung, unbroken since Babylon. In the third court the priestess-dancers work before apparatuses like branching trees strung with ivory pegs: each peg-posture a letter, each dance a book, truths written in movement, copied for millennia. In a corridor he meets, white-haired, Prince Lubovedsky; the brotherhood gathered him too. What he carries out of this valley becomes the Movements; every sacred dance he will stage is a page from this library.
stops.quote: In the strictly defined movements and combinations of the dancers, certain laws are visually reproduced which are intelligible to those who know them. Such dances are called sacred dances.
stops.quote_source: In Search of the Miraculous (Ouspensky), ch. I: Gurdjieff on the temple dances of the east
suggested_refs: The peg-apparatus described in Meetings with Remarkable Men
sources: Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'Prince Yuri Lubovedsky'
In Search of the Miraculous, ch. I

stops.name: The Gobi, stilts against the sand-wind; the death of Soloviev
stops.campa: The Seekers of Truth, full expedition now (professors, engineers, the indestructible Vitvitskaia), strike into the sands to find a city the legends say lies under the Gobi. Against the sand-wind they engineer stilts, planning to walk above the killing layer of blown grit; the sheep that carry their supplies are to become raft and provisions in turn. In the desert's outer scrub a wild camel bites Soloviev; he dies within hours, and they bury the cured drunkard, the truest of brothers, in sand that has no address. The expedition turns back. The desert keeps its city and takes its fee.
suggested_refs: The stilts-and-sheep expedition scheme, Meetings with Remarkable Men

stops.name: Lhasa, the Tibetan years and the second bullet
stops.campa: The legend gives him years on the roof of the world: Lhasa before the British guns, monasteries where he studies the technique of the lamas, a Tibetan marriage, whispers that the Russian agent the British files call the shadowy Buriat is partly him. In 1902, in the mountains, the second stray bullet drops him, again from a quarrel that was not his. Comrades pack his body through the passes and he lies for months at the edge of consciousness beside one of the great Central Asian deserts, nursed back by wind and goat's milk, while armies gather below to break open the country he is leaving.
sources: Life Is Real Only Then, When 'I Am' (the second wound, 1902)
James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth

stops.name: Chiatura, the third bullet, and the ledge above the abyss
stops.campa: Back in the Caucasus in the year of revolutions, near the Chiatura tunnel, he walks into crossfire between Cossacks and Gurian rebels, and the third stray bullet finds him as the fortune-teller of Alexandropol promised. Friends smuggle the bleeding man across half of Asia to the oasis of Yangi Hissar on the rim of the Takla-makan, where he convalesces in the long silence of the desert's edge. There, the canon says, he holds the great review of his life: three bullets, three resurrections. Chance is dismissed as an explanation. Something is either guarding him or collecting on him, and he resolves to find out which.
sources: Life Is Real Only Then, When 'I Am' (the third wound, 1904)

stops.name: Tashkent, the professional hypnotist, and the oath
stops.campa: He sets up in Tashkent as healer, hypnotist, professor of supernatural sciences: curing drunkards and opium-eaters, staging wonders for the colonial parlors, and all the while running his true experiment: the mapping of human suggestibility, the mechanics of the sleep men call waking life. Money pours in; he becomes rich as a fish in water among the credulous. Then, in the autumn of 1911, he stops. He swears the great oath before his own essence: an artificial life, planned in advance, and his hypnotic power never again for his own profit. The magician binds himself, and the teacher becomes possible.
stops.quote: According to the special oath I took, I bound myself in my conscience to lead in some ways an artificial life, modelled upon a programme which had been previously planned in accordance with certain definite principles.
stops.quote_source: The Herald of Coming Good (the special oath of the artificial life, as Gurdjieff recounts it)
suggested_refs: The Herald of Coming Good, first edition 1933
sources: James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth

segments.name: The Teaching in the Two Capitals

stops.name: Moscow: the man from the East arrives
stops.campa: He appears in Moscow as if condensed out of the East: a shaven-headed man of no determinable age with a million rubles, two priceless collections, carpets and Chinese cloisonné, and thirty years of Asia folded behind his eyes. He deals in oil, fish, carpets, anything; commerce is his camouflage and his war chest. Quietly he begins to gather the first pupils, testing them as ore is tested. The mission assumed in Turkestan now opens its European front: to plant in the sleepwalking West the knowledge carried out of the monasteries.

stops.name: St Petersburg: Julia Ostrowska, the countess of the work
stops.campa: In the capital he marries Julia Osipovna Ostrowska, a young Polish woman of great stillness and bearing, whom the pupils will come to regard as a queen without a court. He says of her that she is a very old soul, far along a road most have not yet found. She will follow him through revolution, mountain passes and exile, rule his kitchens like a sacrament, and become in the canon the one human being he treats as an equal companion of the way.
sources: James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth

stops.name: Moscow, the notice of 'The Struggle of the Magicians'
stops.campa: In the winter of the war's first year, a strange notice appears in The Voice of Moscow: a ballet is announced, 'The Struggle of the Magicians,' by a certain G. I. Gurdjieff, a Hindu, says the paper, wrongly. It is bait, cast with precision. In the scenario a school of the white magician stands against a school of the black, and the sacred dances of the East are to be shown to a city that dances toward its own abyss. Among those who clip the notice is a journalist-philosopher just back from India, still hungry: P. D. Ouspensky.
suggested_refs: The Struggle of the Magicians scenario (published 1957)
sources: In Search of the Miraculous, ch. I

stops.name: Moscow, the small café: Gurdjieff and Ouspensky meet
stops.campa: Spring 1915, a small café in a noisy side street: Ouspensky is brought to meet a man of oriental type, no longer young, with a black moustache and piercing eyes, oddly disguised, so it strikes him, as an ordinary dealer. The face, he writes, belongs under a white burnous by a stone mosque, not in this Moscow smoke. They talk of the East, of drugs and dances, of schools. Ouspensky, who has searched India for the miraculous and come home empty, recognizes within an hour that the miraculous has been sitting in a Moscow café, waiting. The canon of the teaching begins its written life at this table.
suggested_refs: In Search of the Miraculous, opening chapter
sources: In Search of the Miraculous, ch. I

stops.name: St Petersburg, the lectures: man is a machine
stops.campa: Through the war winters he shuttles between the capitals, and in Petersburg apartments the system is laid out plank by plank before small, sworn groups: the ray of creation, the food octaves, the four bodies of man, self-remembering. The teaching's first hammer-blow falls here: that man as he is cannot do, that everything happens in him as rain happens, and that only work on oneself, in a school, under conditions, can wake the machine into a man. Ouspensky writes it all down; the notebooks will outlive the empire in whose lamplight they are filled.
stops.quote: Man is a machine. All his deeds, actions, words, thoughts, feelings, convictions, opinions, and habits are the results of external influences, external impressions.
stops.quote_source: In Search of the Miraculous (Ouspensky), the Petersburg talks

stops.name: Finland, the miracle in the country house
stops.campa: At a country house in Finland the experiment Ouspensky begged for is granted. After days of fasting and exercises, in the night, he begins to hear Gurdjieff's voice inside his chest: questions asked and answered with no word spoken aloud in the room. The conversation continues next day across a garden, mind into mind, until Ouspensky, shaken to his foundations, wants to abandon everything and follow like a disciple of Galilee. Gurdjieff closes the channel as calmly as he opened it. In the canon this is the proof-night: the miraculous exists, is lawful, and is expensive.
suggested_refs: In Search of the Miraculous, the Finland chapter
sources: In Search of the Miraculous, ch. XIII

stops.name: Alexandropol, the last spring of the old world
stops.campa: The Tsar falls, and Gurdjieff, reading the avalanche in its first pebbles, leaves Petersburg for his birthplace. He sits again in his parents' courtyard in Alexandropol, drinks coffee with his father under the poplars, mends the family's affairs, and says nothing of what he sees coming. It is the last time. He urges the old ashokh to move to safety; the father, seventy-five spring-times stubborn, will not leave his gates. The son goes north to the mineral towns to gather his pupils out of the fire.

stops.name: Essentuki, the six weeks
stops.campa: In a rented house in the spa town of Essentuki, with a dozen pupils and the empire dissolving beyond the garden wall, he compresses years of school into six weeks: fasts, breathing, the stop exercise that freezes a body mid-gesture like a struck bell, labor past all ordinary limit. He shows them, Ouspensky writes, everything at once, the whole ladder in one furious summer. Nothing counts here but what is paid for above the ordinary rate; the intensive becomes the seed-pattern of every institute he will ever found.
stops.quote: In work only super-efforts are counted, that is, beyond the normal, beyond the necessary; ordinary efforts are not counted.
stops.quote_source: In Search of the Miraculous (Ouspensky), the Essentuki period
sources: In Search of the Miraculous, ch. XVII

stops.name: Tuapse and the Black Sea shore, wandering between armies
stops.campa: He disperses the group and drifts with a handful of the faithful down the Black Sea coast, Tuapse, Uch Dere, renting houses ahead of the collapse, buying and selling to keep the caravan fed. October detonates in the north. Deserters flood the roads; money rots in the wallet. He walks the shore roads with Ostrowska and the de Hartmanns, the composer still in his officer's boots, teaching in kitchens and on cliff paths, unhurried, as though the apocalypse were a weather he had long ago learned to travel in.
suggested_refs: Thomas de Hartmann's memoir of the coast wanderings
sources: Thomas and Olga de Hartmann, Our Life with Mr. Gurdjieff

stops.name: Essentuki, the colony of 1918; the father under the Turkish guns
stops.campa: He summons the scattered by circular letter, and forty come to Essentuki, where the work becomes a commune under siege economics: gymnastics at dawn, fasts, dictations, the household run like a ship in weather. Through the Caucasus wall comes black news: the Turks have broken into Alexandropol, and his father, defending his own gate at seventy-nine, has been shot and lies in a grave no son could attend. Gurdjieff receives it in silence and folds it into the work. Years later he will end his father's chapter with the one filial commandment left him: to honor the grave he could not dig.
suggested_refs: The father's memorial; the closing page of 'My Father'

stops.name: Maikop: the 'scientific expedition' assembles
stops.campa: Civil war closes like a fist, and he performs his masterpiece of practical magic: papers. From the Bolshevik soviet he conjures a mandate for a scientific expedition to Mount Induc, to prospect, the documents say, for gold and antiquities, and two railway cars are placed at the service of citizen Gurdjieff by a power that is shooting men of his kind. The party entrains with alcohol, silk and manuscripts sewn into the baggage: silk for currency where money has died, and the written work, the future books and Movements, rolled among the tent poles.
sources: Thomas and Olga de Hartmann, Our Life with Mr. Gurdjieff
Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'The Material Question'

stops.name: The passes above the sea, through two armies on foot
stops.campa: Beyond Maikop the rails end and the mountains begin. On foot and with pack-horses the party crosses the fighting line five times, Red pickets, White pickets, brigand country between, and at each barrier Gurdjieff produces the paper of the power that holds the road, greeting commissar and colonel each as his own. Bridges are out; loads are carried on backs over gorges; the women walk in boots stuffed with the last money. Not one of the party is lost. In the canon this crossing is a demonstration mounted by the teacher himself: what a man who is awake can walk through.
suggested_refs: The de Hartmanns' account of the mountain crossing
sources: Thomas and Olga de Hartmann, Our Life with Mr. Gurdjieff

stops.name: Sochi: the sea reached, the party sifted
stops.campa: They come down out of the passes to the palms and mud of Sochi, into White-held coast, and the expedition dissolves the way his enterprises always dissolve once their real work is done: the mountain has sorted the pilgrims. Several of the oldest pupils fall away here, kept by families, fears, or their own counsel. He winters on the coast without visible regret: sells silk, doctors the sick, plans forward. The teaching travels light into 1919: Ostrowska, the de Hartmanns, the Stjernvalls, a few more. Enough.
sources: Thomas and Olga de Hartmann, Our Life with Mr. Gurdjieff

stops.name: Tiflis, the Institute founded; the Movements take the Opera stage
stops.campa: In Tiflis, city of his railway youth, the wandering school becomes an Institution: the Institute for the Harmonious Development of Man is founded here first, its prospectus as grand as its treasury is thin. The painter Alexandre de Salzmann and his wife Jeanne, mistress of a Dalcroze studio, join him; to Jeanne's trained dancers he begins to give the sacred movements carried from the Sarmoung valley. On 22 June 1919, at the Tiflis Opera House, the dances written in the hidden monastery are performed on a public stage of Europe's edge for the first time.

segments.name: Between Empires: Constantinople to the West

stops.name: Constantinople, the Institute in Pera
stops.campa: Georgia buckles, and the school ships from Batum to Constantinople, a city between two corpses of empire, swollen with White Russian refugees selling their rings on the Grande Rue. Gurdjieff sells carpets, cures nerve-cases, and within weeks has the Institute running in Pera: movements classes, lectures, the Struggle of the Magicians in rehearsal. Here a young English intelligence officer named John Bennett, watching him move through a crowded room, meets the strangest man he will ever know, and is marked for life without understanding what has touched him.

stops.name: The Mevlevi tekke at Galata, the turning explained
stops.campa: He takes Ouspensky and the pupils to the Mevlevi house at Galata, where the dervishes wheel under the wooden dome, skirts opened into white planets. The visitors see ecstasy; he shows them mathematics. The turning, he explains, is built on counting: exercises of attention hidden inside what Europe calls a dance of trance, the mind held to inner sequences while the body orbits. It is the Sarmoung lesson again, spoken in Ottoman accent: what survives of real knowledge survives disguised as worship, art, and spectacle.
sources: In Search of the Miraculous (the Constantinople period)

stops.name: Berlin, the western foothold that would not hold
stops.campa: Kemal's war closes Anatolia and the school moves again, west into the hungry brilliance of Weimar Berlin. He lectures in Schöneberg halls, negotiates for the famous Dalcroze building at Hellerau outside Dresden, the very temple of European movement-training, which he means to capture for the sacred dances, and is balked by lawsuits and bad faith. Germany, inflation-mad, will not carry the Institute. England beckons through Ouspensky's new London following, but the Home Office bars the master himself. The compass settles on France.
sources: James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth

stops.name: London, the visitation of Ouspensky's group
stops.campa: He descends on London in February 1922 and speaks to the group Ouspensky has built in his name, and over his head. In a Kensington drawing-room packed with editors, doctors and theosophists in recovery, the man himself, in broken and blazing English-through-interpreters, makes his pupils' careful system look like a photograph of a fire. Orage, the most brilliant editor in England, decides on the spot where his life is going. Ouspensky watches his own students turn like compass needles, and the long schism of the canon begins here, politely, over tea.
suggested_refs: A. R. Orage and the New Age circle
sources: James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth
In Search of the Miraculous (final chapters)

stops.name: Paris, arrival with the last of the fortune
stops.campa: He reaches Paris in the high summer of 1922 with his people, his manuscripts and the remains of a fortune worn down by five years of escaping. The Dalcroze school lends its premises; wealthy English pupils, Lady Rothermere's cheque-book at their head, gather the funds the Home Office refused him hospitality. He scouts châteaux like a general choosing ground. The city that will hold his cafés, his crashes and his deathbed receives him without ceremony, one more Russian refugee, as it thinks, among a hundred thousand.
sources: Meetings with Remarkable Men, 'The Material Question'
James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth

stops.name: The Prieuré des Basses Loges, Fontainebleau-Avon: the gates open
stops.campa: On the first of October the Institute for the Harmonious Development of Man takes possession of the Prieuré des Basses Loges at Avon: a prior's estate become a Dreyfus mistress's château, forty-five rooms, fountains, and a wall around a world. The regime begins at once: pupils who were lawyers and countesses dig ditches, fell trees, wash dishes into the night, and are roused before dawn; hard labor is the first language of the teaching. Madame Ostrowska rules the kitchen; the Russians and the English eat at one long table under the master's weather-making eye.

stops.name: The Study House, raised by the pupils' hands
stops.campa: A war-surplus airship hangar is bought, carted to the grounds, and in weeks of day-and-night labor the pupils raise the Study House with their own blistered hands: earth floor covered with carpets from his caravans, a perfumed fountain, painted windows, the aphorisms of the work lettered around the walls in a script devised so that only those taught to read it can. Here the Movements are drilled every evening, the dances of the Sarmoung transplanted into French winter mud, while Gurdjieff sits above on a divan, mending souls, as he says, by making bodies obey.
stops.quote_source: Aphorism inscribed in the Study House at the Prieuré
suggested_refs: Photographs of the Study House interior
sources: C. S. Nott, Teachings of Gurdjieff

stops.name: The cowshed loft, Katherine Mansfield
stops.campa: Katherine Mansfield, the finest short-story writer in English and dying of tuberculosis, arrives in October having chosen the Prieuré over the doctors' sanatoria. Gurdjieff builds her a gallery loft above the cows, de Salzmann painting it with flowers and beasts, and prescribes the old Asian regimen: animal warmth, milk-breath, the watching of simple work. She scrapes carrots in the kitchen, watches the Movements at night, and writes last letters full of a hard new peace: she wants to be all of herself, root and branch. On the ninth of January, climbing the stairs, the hemorrhage comes; she dies within the hour and is buried at Avon.
suggested_refs: Her last letters from the Prieuré

stops.name: Théâtre des Champs-Élysées: Paris sees the sacred dances
stops.campa: From the thirteenth of December the Institute takes the stage of the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, the hall of the Rite of Spring scandal, for public demonstrations of the sacred gymnastics: an orchestra of thirty-five plays the de Hartmann scores, dervish dances and temple movements succeed one another with military exactness, and in the stop exercise dancers hurl themselves at the footlights and are frozen by one word from the dark auditorium, falling and holding like statuary shot from a catapult. Paris, Diaghilev's Paris, does not know whether it has seen art, drill, or liturgy. It has seen the Sarmoung library, opened.
sources: Gurdjieff/de Hartmann, Oriental Suite: The Complete Orchestral Music 1923-1924

stops.name: New York, Carnegie Hall
stops.campa: In January he sails with thirty-five pupils on the S.S. Paris to conquer the New World, Orage sent ahead as herald. Demonstrations mount from Leslie Hall to the summit: on the third of March the sacred dances fill the main stage of Carnegie Hall. America, which measures everything, watches human beings move with a precision it cannot measure, and the harvest is exactly what he came for: the Americans, writers, editors, heiresses, the young Jean Toomer, who will fund and carry the work for the rest of his life. He returns to France in June with the dollar rope that will hold through every coming shipwreck.
suggested_refs: A. R. Orage's New York groups

stops.name: The Paris-Fontainebleau road, the crash
stops.campa: On the night of the eighth of July his Citroën leaves the Paris road at speed and strikes a tree by the forest of Fontainebleau. He is found thrown clear, skull cracked, senseless on the grass, with a seat cushion under his head, placed by no hand anyone can name; the mystery is canon. For days he lies between life and death at the Prieuré, mother and wife at the bed, the pupils moving on tiptoe through a house where the teacher's body burns like a lamp low on oil. The wonder is double: that such a driver crashed at all, and that the crash did not kill him.
sources: Life Is Real Only Then, When 'I Am'

stops.name: Café de la Paix, the office among the waiters
stops.campa: Risen from the crash, he executes the great turn of his life: he clears the Prieuré of half its pupils, dismisses the easy ones, and becomes a writer. His office is a marble table at the Café de la Paix, his staff the waiters who guard his coffee and armagnac; amid the din of the boulevard, he works best, he says, against interruption, as against a grindstone; he fills notebook after notebook in Armenian and Russian with Beelzebub's Tales to His Grandson, a Flood-sized book in which a devil exiled to our solar system explains, to his grandson, everything.
stops.quote: To destroy, mercilessly, without any compromise whatsoever, in the mentation and feelings of the reader, the beliefs and views, by centuries rooted in him, about everything existing in the world.
stops.quote_source: The declared aim of the First Series, All and Everything (Beelzebub's Tales)
suggested_refs: Café de la Paix, Place de l'Opéra
sources: Life Is Real Only Then, When 'I Am'

stops.name: The Prieuré, the two deaths: the mother and Madame Ostrowska
stops.campa: Death walks the Prieuré's alleys twice. His mother, brought out of the Caucasus through the wreck of nations, dies in 1925 and is laid in Avon earth. Then cancer takes hold of Julia Ostrowska, and the doctors give her weeks; Gurdjieff, by regimens and by work no physician can enter into the notes, holds her alive and present month after month past every sentence, the canon counting it among his quiet miracles, until on 26 June 1926 he lets her go. He says she dies as very few know how to die. Something of the Prieuré's sun goes under the ground with her.
suggested_refs: The graves of Evdokia Giorgiades and Julia Ostrowska at Avon
sources: James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth

stops.name: The Prieuré lost
stops.campa: The American crash dries the dollar river; Orage has been recalled and tested and lost to marriage; the mortgages devour the estate. In 1932 the Prieuré passes from his hands, and the seller of a hundred carpets cannot buy back his own decade. He walks out carrying what he came with: manuscripts. The Study House with its painted aphorisms is left to the spiders; the fountain of scent goes dry. In the canon the loss reads as the pattern always reads: the container is broken precisely when the contents have outgrown it. The book is nearly finished, and the book, not the château, was the ark.
suggested_refs: The Prieuré in later ruin; the site today
sources: James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth

segments.name: The Office Among the Waiters: Paris Between the Wars

stops.name: Paris, 'The Herald of Coming Good': the only book he lets loose, then recalls
stops.campa: In the leanest year he publishes the only book of his lifetime, The Herald of Coming Good: part prospectus, part confession, part deliberate stumbling-block, in sentences built like fortifications. In it he tells of the 1911 oath, of hypnotism, of the Institute's aims and his pupils' debts. Then, having sown it, he reverses the gesture no author in Paris can comprehend: he condemns his own book, recalls the copies from circulation, and instructs the pupils that it is not to be read. The canon takes the point as taught: the coming good must be earned, not bought at a kiosk.
suggested_refs: The Herald of Coming Good, Paris 1933 (withdrawn)
sources: James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth

stops.name: Café de la Paix, the Rope
stops.campa: Around his café table gathers the strangest chapter of the teaching: the Rope, a knot of brilliant expatriate women: Kathryn Hulme, Solita Solano, Margaret Anderson, Jane Heap of the Little Review, Elizabeth Gordon, whom he binds together like climbers on one mountain line, telling them that on the inner journey each must haul and be hauled. He teaches them by food, insult, tenderness and exercises given over armagnac at noon; their diaries record a Gurdjieff at full magical strength working in a doll's-house format. Rope by rope, the work learns to live without châteaux.
sources: Solita Solano's notes, Library of Congress

stops.name: 6 rue des Colonels-Renard, the flat
stops.campa: He settles at last into a small second-floor flat near the Étoile, and the whole cosmology shrinks to fit it perfectly: a dining room where fourteen sit in space for six, a pantry crammed like a bazaar warehouse, a cupboard of spices and dried fish from every latitude of his wanderings. Here the ritual form of the late teaching sets: the reading aloud from Beelzebub, the enormous meals cooked by his own hand, the toasts, the sudden surgical question across the table. Brother Dmitri's death and the schisms pass through; the flat holds. It will hold through worse.

stops.name: The Occupation, the full pantry and the toasts to the idiots
stops.campa: Paris starves under the Occupation, and the flat at the Colonels-Renard does not: the pantry stays unaccountably full, and the canon smiles at how shopkeepers extend infinite credit to the old oriental gentleman on the strength of a Texas oil well that exists chiefly in his telling of it; after the war, American pupils' money makes every merchant whole. Nightly through the war years the table is laid, French pupils gathered by Jeanne de Salzmann eat as nowhere else in the city, and the ritual toasts to the idiots ascend their ladder (ordinary, super, arch), the science of self-seeing disguised, once again, as a feast.
stops.quote: To the health of all ordinary idiots.
stops.quote_source: The first toast of the ritual of the idiots, as kept at his table (recorded by Bennett, Hulme, and the Paris groups)
suggested_refs: The ritual of the toasts of the idiots
sources: James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth

stops.name: Near Montargis, the second crash survived
stops.campa: On the road in early August a lorry driven by a drunk smashes into his car near Montargis. An ordinary man of seventy-odd dies in such wreckage; Gurdjieff, ribs staved, black with bruises, lungs filling, is carried home, and that same evening comes to table, sits upright by an act witnesses describe as watching a man rebuild himself joint by joint, and commands the household to serve dinner. Within days he reopens the Movements. The second crash becomes the signal for the last great gathering-in: he sends word that all the scattered groups, Ouspensky's orphans included, are to come to him.
stops.quote: Tonight you come dinner. I must make body work.
stops.quote_source: Spoken to J. G. Bennett on the day of the 1948 crash; recorded in Bennett, Witness

stops.name: New York, the Hotel Wellington winter
stops.campa: In December he crosses to New York for the last American winter and holds court in a suite at the Hotel Wellington: the old American pupils return, Orage's people, the Toomer circle, the children of the Prieuré grown, and new ones crowd the corridor. He cooks for dozens on hotel burners, reads Beelzebub aloud, names his heirs' tasks, and settles the great practical matter: the contract for the publication of Beelzebub's Tales, the ark finally to be launched. To pay for it all he sells, with both hands, the futures he no longer needs. Bravo, America: the word of this visit is harvest.
suggested_refs: The 1950 first edition of Beelzebub's Tales

stops.name: Lascaux, the painted cave read
stops.campa: In the last summer he motors south with pupils, Bennett among them, to the newly opened cave of Lascaux. Bent under the low rock, the old man reads the great aurochs and the swimming stags not as the savants read them but as he read the dances of the Sarmoung: as script. He disputes the scholars' twenty thousand years, dates the work by his own chronology to after the loss of the drowned civilization, and tells Bennett the painters were a brotherhood leaving a message for those able to receive it. The seeker's last expedition is to the oldest library he ever entered.
suggested_refs: The Hall of the Bulls, Lascaux
Bennett's account of the Lascaux visit
sources: James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth

stops.name: Salle Pleyel, the last Movements class
stops.campa: Through October the body visibly founders, the legs swollen tight, the skin gone grey, and still he comes to the Salle Pleyel and drives the Movements classes from his chair, cane striking the floor, building the new series meant for the film that will preserve the dances when he is gone. Pupils see him gather force for each command out of nowhere that medicine knows about. The last class is held days before the end: the library of the Sarmoung, transmitted to the final shelf, in a rented Paris rehearsal hall, by a dying man counting the beat.

stops.name: The American Hospital, Neuilly: the death
stops.campa: Carried at last to the American Hospital, he sits upright on the stretcher, smoking, blessing the household with 'au revoir, tout le monde'; he receives the tapping of the dropsy and the verdict without interest, and to the pupils crowding the room he delivers the final teaching in one sentence, leaving them, with perfect deliberateness, in a fine mess: orphaned into responsibility. On the morning of 29 October 1949 the heart stops. The doctor who attends him testifies he has never seen a man die so consciously; the room, witnesses say, does not feel like a place where something has ended.
stops.quote: Vous voilà dans de beaux draps.
stops.quote_source: His words to the assembled pupils in his last days at the American Hospital, as remembered by those present
suggested_refs: The American Hospital of Paris, Neuilly
Dr. William Welch, 'The Death of Gurdjieff'

stops.name: Avon, the vigil and the grave near the Prieuré
stops.campa: Embalmed after the Russian custom, he lies in state in the hospital's garden chapel while pupils keep unbroken vigil; those who watch report the body does not seem vacated. The funeral fills the Russian cathedral in the rue Daru past its doors, the choir singing over a congregation of every nation he ever taught. Then Avon receives him, a few hundred steps from the Prieuré's wall, beside Ostrowska, his mother, Katherine Mansfield: two rough standing stones at head and foot, no name needed. The mother's slab nearby carries the sentence that closes the canon: here lies the mother of one whom this death compelled to write Beelzebub's Tales.
suggested_refs: Gurdjieff's grave with its two menhirs, Avon cemetery
Cathedral of Saint Alexandre Nevsky, rue Daru
sources: James Moore, Gurdjieff: The Anatomy of a Myth
